Triggers.value: A specific temperature on the skin

Maladaptive Strategies.value: push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe
try hard not think about the trauma
Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events

Threat.value: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order

Negative Appraisals.value: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
There is something wrong with me as a person
I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

issues.item: Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: These items imply a trauma involving a direct interpersonal assault by a perpetrator with ongoing home-intrusion danger. That is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of witnessed other trauma, where the patient observed trauma happening to someone else rather than being personally harmed.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
issues.explanation: The rest of the profile is broadly coherent for PTSD with strong links among triggers, threat, appraisals, and memory, but these two items specifically shift the narrative to a victim-of-assault formulation rather than a witness formulation.

vignette:
For most of his career, Arun had been known as the kind of surgeon who stayed steady when everyone else in the operating room grew tense. At 77, still working in a limited but active role, he took pride in precision, restraint, and the disciplined habits that had shaped decades of practice. The event that now occupied him in fragments happened in a hospital setting much like the one he still entered each week. He had witnessed another person undergo a catastrophic traumatic injury, and what stayed with him was not a single clean memory but scattered sensory moments: the abrupt change in the room, the smell of something burnt, the feel of temperature against his skin, the sharp eruption of noise and alarm. Even when he tried to recount it, the sequence would not settle. He would begin in one place, stop, correct himself, and then say that perhaps that was not first after all. At times he spoke as if the memory belonged to another surgeon, another old man in scrubs, and yet his body answered as though it were happening again.

In the weeks afterward, Arun did what had always served him before: he tried to contain it. He pushed the whole event away whenever it approached his mind. If an image, or more often the beginning of one, stirred, he would deliberately redirect himself, focus on a chart, on laboratory values, on the practical demands of the day. What unsettled him was that often there was no image at all. Instead, a wave of the same emotional force would surge through him without warning, complete and overwhelming, while his mind remained blank. He found this particularly disturbing. It seemed to him like evidence that something in him had become disordered, that there was something wrong with him as a person if he could feel such terror and urgency without even being able to tell himself clearly what he was remembering.

As months passed, the hospital itself became full of moments he could not trust. A particular temperature on his skin could do it: the sudden chill of overair-conditioned corridors, or a patch of unexpected warmth near equipment, and his body would tighten before he had consciously noticed why. The smell of something burnt was even worse. In a surgical environment, cautery and overheated machinery were not rare, and when that smell reached him he became instantly watchful, his attention snapping toward danger. Stress alone could prime the same state. On busy days, when decisions stacked up and voices sharpened, he found himself on edge long before anything actually happened. Unexpected loud sounds in the operating suite or even a dropped instrument made him start violently. He had become a man listening for disaster. He had come to believe that he had to be especially careful because one never knew what might happen next, and he no longer trusted his own body; it seemed to react as if danger were present even in objectively safe situations.

At home, his wife noticed the narrowing of his life before he named it himself. Arun stopped watching films or television shows that involved hospitals, accidents, emergencies, or even dramatic tension that felt too close to catastrophe. If a news segment hinted at injury or fire, he muted it or left the room. He also became wary of feeling too happy or relaxed. Pleasant evenings with his wife, family celebrations, moments of lightness after a good day at the hospital all felt strangely unsafe, as though letting down his guard invited something terrible to break in. He would pull back from those moments, become quiet, find a task to do, or retreat into professional detachment. His wife experienced this as distance, a flattening that neither of them could easily explain.

There were also times when his colleagues saw a different change. Arun, usually deliberate, could become surprisingly reckless in small but noticeable ways: hurrying through hospital corridors, taking on physically taxing responsibilities that younger surgeons could have handled, driving home too fast after long days. He did not describe these moments as wanting harm, but as a restless disregard, as if carefulness no longer guaranteed anything and so caution had lost its meaning. Even then, a slammed door or sudden overhead announcement could make him jump.

By the time he sought help, Arun was exhausted by the effort of managing what he could not organize in his own mind. He said that the worst part was not only fear, but estrangement: the sense that the event was both his and not his, that his body knew it while his mind could not place it in order. He came at his wife's urging after another evening when the smell of burnt food from the kitchen left him shaken and irritable, followed by embarrassment he could not hide. What frightened him most was the idea that he had become fundamentally altered, an aging surgeon whose body would keep sounding alarms long after the danger had passed. What he hoped for, quietly and with some skepticism, was not to forget, but to feel that the memory was his own again and that he could move through the hospital, and his home, without bracing for the next blow.
